section_title: Occupiers, Statutory Duty, Nuisance and Strict Liability

nodes.label: Occupiers, Statutory Duty, Nuisance and Strict Liability
nodes.summary: Occupiers' liability to entrants, breach of statutory duty as tort, private and public nuisance, the rule in Rylands v Fletcher, and strict liability for animals.

nodes.label: Occupiers' Liability Overview
nodes.summary: Hong Kong occupiers' liability is governed by the Occupiers' Liability Ordinance (Cap. 314) for lawful visitors, including the common duty of care, with residual/common-law issues requiring verification for trespassers and related categories.

nodes.label: Definition of Occupier
nodes.summary: An occupier is a person who has a sufficient degree of control over premises. More than one person may be an occupier (landlord, tenant, contractor with control).

nodes.label: Common Duty of Care and Entrant Categories
nodes.summary: For lawful visitors, the Occupiers' Liability Ordinance (Cap. 314) provides a common duty of care. Any residual treatment of trespassers, implied permission, child entrants, landlord control, and older common-law categories should remain source-checked against HK authority.

nodes.label: Child Entrants and Allurement
nodes.summary: A higher standard of care may be owed to child entrants if there is an allurement or trap that attracts children. The occupier must anticipate children's lack of appreciation of danger.

nodes.label: Landlord's Liability
nodes.summary: A landlord may be liable as occupier where they retain control over common parts. Liability for latent defects existing at the time of letting requires proof of knowledge.

nodes.label: Breach of Statutory Duty as Tort
nodes.summary: Breach of a statutory duty may be actionable in tort if: (a) the statute confers a private right of action, (b) the claimant is within the class of persons protected, and (c) the injury is of the kind the statute intended to prevent.

nodes.label: Nuisance Overview
nodes.summary: Nuisance protects against unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land or public rights. Divided into private nuisance (land interests) and public nuisance (common rights).

nodes.label: Private Nuisance
nodes.summary: A substantial and unreasonable interference with the claimant's use or enjoyment of land. Requires the claimant to have an interest in the land. Factors: locality, duration, sensitivity, malice, social utility.

nodes.label: Public Nuisance
nodes.summary: An act or omission that materially affects the public's common rights (highway obstruction, polluting a waterway). Actionable in tort only if the claimant suffers particular damage beyond the general public.

nodes.label: Who May Be Sued in Nuisance
nodes.summary: The creator of the nuisance (occupier or not) may be liable. An occupier who adopts or continues a nuisance created by a third party may also be liable. Landlord liable only if they authorised the nuisance.

nodes.label: Defences to Nuisance
nodes.summary: Statutory authority (express or implied), prescription (20 years continuous use), consent/coming to the nuisance (weak defence), and reasonable user (negates unreasonableness).

nodes.label: The Rule in Rylands v Fletcher
nodes.summary: Strict liability for escape of dangerous things from land: a person who brings or accumulates anything likely to do mischief if it escapes does so at their peril. Requires: (1) accumulation, (2) escape, (3) non-natural use, (4) mischief.

nodes.label: Non-Natural Use of Land
nodes.summary: Non-natural use is a special use bringing increased danger to others. Not determined solely by whether the use is ordinary. Storage of water, gas, electricity, chemicals in quantity may qualify. HK position needs verification.

nodes.label: Defences to Rylands v Fletcher
nodes.summary: Consent of the claimant, common benefit, act of God, act of a stranger (no control), statutory authority, and default of the claimant.

nodes.label: Animals / Scienter
nodes.summary: Strict liability for damage caused by dangerous animals (scienter action) and for cattle trespass. Keepers of wild animals are strictly liable. Knowledge of dangerousness is presumed for wild animals; must be proved for domestic animals.

nodes.label: Hui Kin Sing v Chan Chi Keung [2015] HKCFI 234
nodes.summary: Seed case for private nuisance in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Rylands v Fletcher (1868) LR 3 HL 330
nodes.summary: Foundational strict liability rule for escape of dangerous things. Person who brings dangerous thing onto land is strictly liable for escape causing damage.

nodes.label: Occupiers' Liability Ordinance (Cap. 314)
nodes.summary: Statutory anchor for Hong Kong occupiers' liability, including the common duty of care for lawful visitors. Exact sections, wording, and treatment of non-visitors require official-source verification.

nodes.label: Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather plc [1994] 2 AC 264
nodes.summary: Modern Rylands v Fletcher: foreseeability of damage of the relevant type is required. Narrowed the scope of non-natural use.

nodes.label: Verify HK Occupiers' Liability Statutory and Residual Common Law
nodes.summary: Confirm the current text and interpretation of the Occupiers' Liability Ordinance (Cap. 314), including the common duty of care, s.3/s.6 issues if applicable, and any residual/common-law treatment of trespassers or special entrant categories.
